growth_story.headline: Guatemala: after the lost 1980s, three decades of steady but modest gains, with income per person at a new high in 2025 and remittances carrying demand
growth_story.arc: Income per person in Guatemala fell from 1980 to 1986 and did not pass its 1980 level again until 2006. The World Bank traces that loss to war, inflation and economic mismanagement in the 1980s, and credits peace and better policies with the recovery of the 1990s. Since 1990 the data show one long era with no lasting shift: growth in income per person averaged 1.5 percent a year over 1990–2025. The dips inside it were short, in 2009 during the global financial crisis (-1.5 percent) and in the pandemic year 2020 (-3.2 percent), followed by a 6.6 percent rebound in 2021. Growth edged up from 1.7 percent a year over 2006–2015 to 1.9 percent over 2016–2025, and income per person reached a new peak in 2025. Recent sources tie this pace to careful budget and monetary management and to money sent home by Guatemalans abroad, which now drives household spending.

threads.title: War and the lost 1980s
threads.text: Military rule, civil war and high inflation pushed income per person down after 1980. It fell every year from 1981 to 1986 and took until 2006 to pass its 1980 level.

citations.title: Guatemala Country Assistance Evaluation (Report No. 25212-GT)
citations.quote: Inflation, economic decline, and civil war impoverished Guatemalans in the 1980s, but good economic performance during the 1990s improved their welfare.

citations.title: Guatemala Country Assistance Evaluation (Report No. 25212-GT)
citations.quote: The last era of military rule (1954-1985) brought some initial prosperity, but ended in misery and intense violence.

citations.title: Guatemala Country Assistance Evaluation (Report No. 25212-GT)
citations.quote: Real GDP per capita in 1985 fell 20 percent below the 1980 peak, which has not been reached again

threads.title: Peace, then steady slow growth
threads.text: The 1996 peace accords ended more than three decades of internal conflict and brought more stability, but growth after them stayed slow and steady rather than fast. Growth was held back again around 2009 by the global financial crisis, and two natural disasters hit in 2010.

citations.title: Guatemala Constraints Analysis Report 2013
citations.quote: Following the end of its three decades of internal conflict in 1996, Guatemala has grown steadily but slowly (1.3 percent per capita annually)

citations.title: Guatemala Constraints Analysis Report 2013
citations.quote: a modest rate in part due to the global financial crisis and two natural disasters in 2010.

threads.title: Remittances drive spending
threads.text: Money sent home by Guatemalans living abroad now drives household spending and supports the external accounts. The IMF notes that these inflows also weigh on competitiveness, and it warned in 2025 that a proposed US tax on remittances could disrupt the spending they support.

citations.title: Guatemala: Macro Poverty Outlook, October 2026
citations.quote: At about a fifth of GDP, remittance inflows drive domestic demand and support external balances and reserve accumulation.

citations.title: IMF Executive Board Concludes 2026 Article IV Consultation with Guatemala
citations.quote: Large remittance inflows support consumption but complicate monetary management and weigh on competitiveness.

citations.title: Guatemala: Staff Concluding Statement of the 2025 Article IV Mission
citations.quote: proposed 3.5 percent excise tax on remittances in U.S. policy discussions could disrupt remittance-supported consumption

threads.title: Careful management, thin investment
threads.text: The World Bank credits careful budget and monetary management for the steady record, and public debt stays low. Investment is low for Guatemala's income level, at 16.3 percent of GDP, though the World Bank expects fixed investment to pick up as infrastructure projects move ahead.

citations.title: Guatemala: Macro Poverty Outlook, October 2026
citations.quote: Guatemala's economy grew by an average of 3.6 percent annually during 2015–2025, buttressed by prudent macroeconomic and fiscal management

citations.title: Guatemala: Macro Poverty Outlook, October 2026
citations.quote: Public debt remained low at 26.1 percent of GDP.

citations.title: Guatemala: Macro Poverty Outlook, October 2026
citations.quote: Fixed investment, however, is forecast to pick up as infrastructure projects advance.

since_last_year.text: Income per person grew 2.7 percent in 2025 and reached a new high. Remittances hit a record that year, and growth sped up again in early 2026. The World Bank expects growth to slow over 2026–2028 as spending driven by remittances eases.

citations.title: IMF Executive Board Concludes 2026 Article IV Consultation with Guatemala
citations.quote: The 2025 current account surplus reached 4.7 percent of GDP; remittances reached a record-high 21 percent of GDP.

citations.title: Guatemala: Macro Poverty Outlook, October 2026
citations.quote: Growth accelerated to 4.5 percent in Q1 2026 from 3.8 percent a year earlier.

citations.title: Guatemala: Macro Poverty Outlook, October 2026
citations.quote: Growth is projected to slow to an average of 3.8 percent over 2026–2028 as remittance-driven private consumption moderates.

growth_story.tension: The World Bank describes a decade of sustained growth for the whole economy, helped by a young and expanding labor force, yet income per person grew only 1.9 percent a year over 2016–2025. A fast-growing population takes a large share of each year's gain, which is why Guatemala's steady growth has closed income gaps slowly.
